scenario_stem:
Braeburn Valley Wholesale Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying frozen and dry goods to 14 independent shops. Run by managing director Karen Doyle for 6 years, it earned revenue of $1.15 million last year with a profit of $92,000. Current assets are $180,000 (inventories $96,000, trade receivables $64,000 and cash $20,000) while current liabilities are $120,000, made up of trade payables of $72,000 and a bank overdraft of $48,000.

Braeburn's largest supplier, Delta Produce, offers 30-day credit, and a regional supermarket group, FreshMart, has offered a contract worth $260,000 a year in extra sales if Braeburn can hold more stock and give 45 days to pay. Karen must decide whether to accept the FreshMart contract or keep supplying the 14 independent shops, which pay within 14 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets divided by current liabilities; it shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts when they fall due, expressed as x:1 [2].

knowledge_max_2: current assets divided by current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Karen should study the acid test ratio before accepting the FreshMart contract.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The acid test is a stricter measure of liquidity than the current ratio [k]; Braeburn's acid test is 0.7:1, that is ($180,000 - $96,000) / $120,000, well below the 1.5:1 current ratio [app]. Reason 2: The acid test ignores inventories, which can be slow to sell [k]; Braeburn holds $96,000 of inventories within $180,000 current assets, and the FreshMart deal needs still more stock plus 45 days for FreshMart to pay [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of Braeburn's final accounts for its stakeholders.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The bank can use the final accounts to judge whether to lend or renew the $48,000 overdraft [k]; with working capital of only $60,000 ($180,000 - $120,000) and an acid test of 0.7:1, the bank can see cash is tight, so it may demand security or restrict the facility [app][an]. Use 2: Delta Produce can use the final accounts to set credit terms before the FreshMart deal [k]; trade payables of $72,000 against current assets of $180,000 show how much Braeburn already owes suppliers, so Delta Produce can decide whether to keep 30-day terms or tighten them [app][an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Karen should accept the FreshMart contract? Justify your answer.

Current assets total $150,000 (inventories $30,000, trade receivables $30,000 and bank balance $90,000); current liabilities total $75,000 (trade payables $45,000 and a bank overdraft of $30,000). Occupancy falls to 35% between November and March.

scenario_stem:
Duncannon Timber Homes Ltd manufactures timber-frame house kits in Country X. Director Adam Kowalski took over the business 9 years ago; last year's revenue was $3.4 million, up from $3.0 million the year before. This year's current assets are $260,000 (inventories $140,000, trade receivables $85,000 and cash $35,000) with current liabilities of $130,000; last year current assets were $200,000 (inventories $90,000) and current liabilities $100,000.

A national housing association has offered a $900,000 contract to supply 60 timber-frame kits, but it requires Duncannon to hold far more timber in stock from March. Adam must decide whether to accept the contract, or stay with private housebuilders paying within 30 days. Inflation has pushed timber prices up sharply over the last two years.

Use 2: Directors use ratio analysis to help decide whether to accept the housing association contract [k]; if required stocks of timber rise well beyond $140,000, the acid test could fall sharply, so Adam can insist on phased deliveries before signing [app].

Limitation 2: Comparisons over time are distorted by inflation and price changes [k]; timber prices have pushed inventories from $90,000 to $140,000, so higher stock value does not necessarily mean more timber in real terms [app][an].

Last year the current ratio was 2.0:1 and the acid test about 0.92:1; this year they are 2.2:1 and 1.0:1.

scenario_stem:
Caldmoor Bay Holiday Camp is a private limited company in Country X running a 140-pitch seaside campsite with swimming pools and restaurants, directed by owner Martin Hollis. Revenue last year was $1.9 million, mostly between May and September; 25 staff are full-time and 35 are seasonal. Current assets are $320,000 (inventories $80,000, trade receivables $35,000 and cash $205,000) against current liabilities of $160,000. In February last year current assets were $190,000 (inventories $60,000) and current liabilities were $150,000.

Martin must decide whether to invest $280,000 in heated indoor pools and winter events to open all year, or keep the 7-month season and accept winter closures. The bank will consider a winter overdraft of up to $120,000. Employees want year-round jobs; the owners fear an overdraft spiral in winter.
